summary: Defines the LDAP Assertion Control, letting a client say an operation should only be processed if an assertion about the target entry is true. It can build test-and-set, test-and-clear and other conditional operations. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Only change the sign if it still says what I think it says. If someone else changed it, do nothing.

questions: what is the ldap assertion control
how to do test and set in ldap
what is the oid of the ldap assertion control
subtitle: Make an LDAP operation happen only if a filter about the target entry is true, as one atomic step.

tldr.problem: A directory client that reads an entry and then updates it can be undone by someone else changing the entry in between. Clients need a way to say that an operation should only run if the entry still looks the way they expect.
tldr.mechanism: The assertion control carries an LDAP filter. The server evaluates it against the target entry as part of the operation. If it is TRUE the operation proceeds normally; if it is FALSE or Undefined the server returns assertionFailed (122) and does nothing more.
tldr.outcome: Clients can build atomic test-and-set, test-and-clear and other conditional operations. It is a Proposed Standard, and servers should put access and administrative controls around it.

today: RFC 4528 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was published in June 2006 and is referenced by the read entry controls in RFC 4527.

sections.title: A Condition Attached to an Operation
sections.content:
RFC 4528 defines the assertion control for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It lets a client specify a condition that must be true for the operation to be processed normally. Otherwise the operation is not performed.

With the Modify operation, for example, the control can perform atomic test and set and test and clear operations. It may be attached to any update operation to support conditional addition, deletion, modification and renaming of the target object, and the condition is evaluated as an integral part of the operation.

It can also be used with Search, where the assertion is applied to the base object before searching for matching objects, and with Compare, where it extends the operation to allow a more complex assertion.
sections.eli5: You add a rule to your request: do this only if things are still the way I think they are. If the rule is not true, nothing happens.

sections.title: The Assertion Control
sections.content:
The assertion control is an LDAP control whose controlType is 1.3.6.1.1.12 and whose controlValue is a BER-encoded Filter, the same kind of filter used in searches. The criticality may be TRUE or FALSE. There is no corresponding response control.

It is appropriate for both interrogation and update operations: Add, Compare, Delete, Modify, ModifyDN (rename) and Search. It is inappropriate for Abandon, Bind, Unbind and StartTLS.

Servers implementing it SHOULD publish 1.3.6.1.1.12 as a value of the supportedControl attribute in their root DSE. A server MAY advertise the extension only to clients that are authorized to use it.
sections.eli5: The rule is written in the same style as a search question, such as: does this entry have this value? It has its own official number, so servers know what it is.

sections.title: How the Target Is Chosen and Tested
sections.content:
The filter is applied against the target of the operation. For Add, Compare and ModifyDN the target is the entry field of the request. For Modify it is the object field. For Delete it is the DelRequest type. For Search it is the baseObject field.

For Compare and all update operations, the evaluation of the assertion MUST be performed as an integral part of the operation: the evaluation and the normal processing SHALL be one atomic action. For Search, the evaluation is done after finding the base object but before searching, so no entries or continuation references are returned if the assertion fails.

Other documents may extend the control to other operations, and when they do they must state how the target entry is determined.
sections.eli5: The check looks at the one thing your request is about. The check and the change happen together, so nobody can change it between the check and the action.

sections.title: When the Assertion Fails
sections.content:
If the filter evaluates to TRUE, the request is processed normally. If it evaluates to FALSE or Undefined, the server returns the assertionFailed result code (122) and performs no further processing.

IANA assigned assertionFailed (122) as a new LDAP result code for this purpose.
sections.eli5: If the rule is not true, or the server cannot tell, it says assertion failed and leaves everything as it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The filter may, like other parts of a request, contain sensitive information, and when it does it should be appropriately protected. Because any general assertion mechanism can be used to determine directory content, this mechanism SHOULD be subject to appropriate access controls.

Some assertions may be very complex and need significant time and resources to evaluate, so the mechanism SHOULD also be subject to appropriate administrative controls. The considerations of RFC 4511 and the general LDAP considerations of RFC 4510 also apply.
sections.eli5: Someone could keep asking yes-or-no questions to learn what is in the directory, or ask very hard questions to tire the server out. So the server should limit who can do this.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned an LDAP object identifier to identify the assertion control and the result code assertionFailed (122). The document also asks for registration of the protocol mechanism with object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.12, description Assertion Control and usage Control. The change controller is the IESG.
sections.eli5: The control and its failure message were given official numbers in a public list.
